title: Lasso raises $30M and ships an AI guardrail that runs on plain CPUs
subtitle: LEAP is a transformer-free classifier that Lasso claims decides in under five milliseconds — moving guardrail inference off GPU infrastructure entirely.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Lasso Security on September 2 announced a $30 million funding round led by ClearSky, with Entrée Capital, iAngels, Singtel Innov8, Mindset, and Swish Data participating — bringing Lasso's total funding to more than $37 million. Alongside the round, the Tel Aviv and New York company launched LEAP, a guardrail engine that Lasso says delivers top-tier detection accuracy on ordinary CPUs, no GPU required, at under five milliseconds per decision and thousands of times the throughput of existing guardrails.

The technical claim is what makes this newsworthy. Most production guardrails today are small transformer classifiers that need at least a slice of GPU to hit acceptable latency, which pushes cost and deployment complexity onto every application that filters model input or output. A transformer-free classifier that runs at sub-five-millisecond latency on commodity CPUs would let a guardrail sit inline on every request without the GPU footprint of the model it protects — the difference between a filter you can afford to always turn on and one you have to reserve for suspicious traffic.

The funding will pay for engineering hires in Tel Aviv and New York and a push into federal and regulated-industry accounts, plus wider sales coverage in North America and Europe. The round lands in a market that is rapidly separating from generic application security: JetStream shipped its Clearance pre-action authorization engine the same day, Cloudflare has been building AI-specific edge controls, and enterprise buyers now expect a distinct AI-security line item rather than a bolt-on to an existing WAF.

Takeaway for learners: cost per decision determines where a security control can actually run. A guardrail priced by GPU-seconds gets used sparingly; one that runs in milliseconds on the CPU that was already going to handle the HTTP request gets used on everything. Watch this pattern — moving a workload off specialized hardware and back onto commodity CPUs — because it is one of the clearest ways a new AI subsystem goes from a premium add-on to infrastructure that ships by default.
